rationale: A wins because it keeps the sharpest product fact clean: "Going's new AI planner lets the airfare pick the destination" is a real inversion from the update. B has good bones, but "turns a $200 mistake fare into a booked week" smuggles in a fake fare and implies booking the update explicitly says does not happen in-app. That is how a pitch gets killed after one editor asks, "says who?"
gaps_in_A: "Going puts its AI planner behind the paywall to convert 2 million free deal-hunters" states motive too hard. The facts support Premium-only plus a 2 million free audience; conversion is the hypothesis, not a proved intent.
"Not for ... product-review columns" cuts too broadly. A consumer-service angle testing whether Premium is worth paying for is valid, especially because the planner links out and does not book.
"The word 'yet' in the company's own description means this window may close on the company's own roadmap" overreads one word. Keep the roadmap as a question unless Going will answer it on record.
gaps_in_B: "turns a $200 mistake fare into a booked week" is invented and careless. No $200 fare was supplied, and "booked week" fights the fact that no airline or hotel booking happens in-app.

"the free tier finds the fare, the paid tier tells you what to do with it" overstates the tier mechanics. The update says the app finds fares and the planner is Premium-only; it does not say free users receive the same fare and then hit a planning wall.
"against free alternatives their readers already use" and "free general-purpose chatbot" import competitor context that was not in the update. Fine as a proof question, sloppy as the angle's spine.

"Next step: newsjack-detector" is the wrong first move for this set. The founder needs proof and journalist fit on a chosen angle, not a scavenger hunt for a stronger peg after the launch has already happened.
